originalEnglish:
creating chemistry
Chemistry is the perceptible, energetic relationship between two or more individuals on screen. Chemistry is a valuable
asset to building authenticity and believability, increasing the emotional impact of a film.
Energy isn’t a token deliverable like image or sound, so it is tricky to convey and carry through to the audience.
Magical moments between actors are fleeting. Rhythm is delicate and difficult to maintain in the edit. Small details can
subliminally impact audiences, breaking the illusion. The subtlety of human expression is tricky to capture.

So, how do we preserve chemistry?
genre
Romance films fall into 3 categories: classic, tragedy & comedy. We’ll speak in terms of romantic relationships, but the
same tools can be used for any type of relationship.

Classic romance: Two soulmates are challenged by an exterior force that keep them apart, but they defeat it and end
up together in the end. Films with platonic or familial soulmates often take the form of adventure, sports drama or
triumphant character study.

Tragic romance: Two soulmates are challenged by an exterior force that ultimately tears them apart. Films with
platonic or familial soulmates often take the form of thriller, bittersweet character study or family drama.

Romantic comedy: Two soulmates are kept apart by their own personal, internal conflicts that keep them at odds
until they grow and change. When the two soulmates are platonic, we call it a buddy comedy.
Knowing this, we can intentionally create cinematic moments that communicate connectedness or disharmony
depending on the moment in the story we are in.


                                             A classic romance has 3 distinct peaks
                                                       and valleys of connectivity, the height
                                                                      of their connection peaking at the end
                                                                      of the film.





                                                              In a tragic romance, the height of
                                                                    connectivity typically peaks in the first
                                                                             half, and certainly before the 3rd act.
                                                     Deep valleys create a dysfunctional,
                                                                       rollercoaster effect. A steady build
                                                              with a sharp drop off will focus the
                                                            impact on the tragic separation.

chemistry visualizing techniques
connect the dots
To strengthen a connection, use elements in the background of your composition to draw a line from
one character to the other.




unified framing
To unify two or more characters, use a single background element to frame them together.





divided framing
To disconnect two characters, use background elements to divide the composition, framing them
apart from each other.

eyelines
Characters looking in the same direction communicate a sense of unified purpose or intention.
Characters looking in different directions communicate differing intentions, creating disconnection
or a sense of going seperate ways.





 unity                                       tension
eye level
The more aligned the characters eye level, the more we see them on the same page. This literally
conveys they see each other, are connected, and share a unified state of mind. Disperate eye levels
communicates different perspectives, create a feeling of tension or disharmony.





 unity                                       tension

grouping
Characters together in a singe unit imply implicit connection. Separating groups show an audience each
character’s subliminal or explicit relationships to one another.

overlapping
Overlapping two or more characters causes your audience to take them in as a singular unit.
Distancing two or more chararacters will accentuate the space between them.





 unity                                       tension

proximity vs spacing

Proximity is the perceivable physical distance between two actors in the 3-dimensional space.

Spacing is the 2-dimensional distance between two figures in a composition.

Where you place the camera will either accentuate or deemphasize the physical proximity
between two characters.

Characters who are physically distant can be visually connected with close compositional
spacing.





 proximity                                 spacing

characters will reinforce the closeness of
their relationship. Additionally, you can
employ the symbolic meaning the shapes

together, apart
Characters can’t be together all the time, but chemistry between characters is still communicated
when shot individually. Here are techniques to maintain the connectivity of characters throughout
the duration of a movie.
repeated postures
Filming characters in similar postures suggests a connection or relationship between them.





repeated framing
Filming characters in the same exact composition suggests a thematic connection between them.





up close and personal
Extreme closeups can denote a personal connection by showcasing details that only intimate partners
could observe, strengthening the audiences connection to them.





 proximity                                 spacing

mise en scène
Costumes, set design, and lighting affect how your characters and their relationships are percieved.
costuming
Costumes communicate a great deal about your character’s habits and frame of mind. Color, pattern,
silhouette, style, attention to detail, and signature identifiers are some of the qualities that present a
character, and compare them to others in their world.

                        color & pattern
                                           Differences in color, pattern & texture invite direct comparison. Sameness
                                    communicates a reflection or connection. Difference communicates
                                         opposition or disconnection. See how in Call Me By Your Name, both
                                           characters wear a blue, striped, collared short-sleeved shirt to convey that
                                            Elio sees himself in Oliver.

                          unified styling
                                  You can communicate that characters belong together by unifying their
                                      costumes and styling. Think of a partnership wearing clothes from the same
                                                 closet, with a unified color pallette and compatible textures. In The Birdcage
                                we easily read that Albert & Armand are a married couple. Conversely,
                                           characters who don’t belong together might look like they shop at different
                                            stores entirely.
                     group identifiers
                                   Keep characters connected with subtle or explicit identifiers. Think of them
                                       having a shared uniform that sets them apart from all the other characters.
                                        In Jurassic Park we stay aware that Dr. Grant & Dr. Sattler are partners with
                                           saturate colors, rolled cuffs, and defined waistlines.

                          silhouettes
                                            Silhouettes have a strong impact on your composition. They communicate
                                       a great deal about time, place & lifestyle, and will have a part in
                                     communicating similarities or differences between characters. In Bill & Ted’s
                                           Excellent Adventure, Bill & Ted maintain very similar silhouettes, keeping
                                  them connected to each other and distinct from Socrates, Sigmund Freud,
                                      Genghis Khan and Beethoven.
                       repeated choices
                                          Just like in your compositions, you can keep characters connected with
                                         repeated motifs. Here in Little Women, Jo wears an outfit of similar color
                                   and styling to something her mother wore in her own way in a previous
                                           scene.

environment
Environments shape our subliminal perception of the characters that occupy them. Use the
following techniques to communicate aspects of yur character’s relationship through location
and production design.

organic shapes
Rounded, natural lines and shapes suggest intimacy, humanity, ease and safety.





hard lines
Linear shapes, angles, and hard edges suggest coldness, removal, and impartiality.





lighting
Characters which share a single light source often feel connected to each other. Characters lit in
different or opposing lighting patterns are suggested to be at odds with each other.

2. recreate a scene from your life

Think of a memory from your own life in which you met someone important to
you for the first time. Use the following prompts to recall specific details:


What environment did you meet in? What was the lighting and mood of that space?

Did you stand or sit close to each other, or far away?

Did you hit it off at first, or did you need time to warm up to each other?


Now think of the last time you saw this person.


What environment were you in? What was the lighting and mood of that space?

Did you stand or sit close to each other, or far away?

How did this encounter differ from your first memory of the person?


Use these memories to write, storyboard, or conceptualize a scene in a film about
these events, then use the details you recall to create more chemistry between
the characters.


3. transpose documentary to narrative fiction

Watch a scene from a documentary that involves two or more characters.

Carefully observe each person’s interactions, and correlate them to the chemistry techniques
from this course. Do you naturally observe any of these trends within the real life scene?

Record what you find, and transpose any observations to a scene you are working on in a
narrative project.
